  A hash map is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and provides very fast lookup, insertion, and deletion, typically in constant time on average. It works by passing each key through a hash function, which converts the key into an integer. That integer is then mapped to an index in an underlying array, often called a bucket array, where the value is stored. Because different keys can produce the same index, a situation called a collision, hash maps use strategies such as chaining, where each bucket holds a small list, or open addressing, where another free slot is probed. When the array becomes too full, the map resizes and rehashes its entries to keep operations fast. Keys must be hashable and comparable for equality.

When too full, the map resizes and rehashes. Keys must be hashable and comparable.
